item.title: Rotonium Unveils a Quantum Computer That Operates at Room Temperature
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it demonstrates a fully room‑temperature photonic quantum processor, eliminating the bulky cryogenics that have long constrained superconducting platforms and limiting system cost and footprint. By integrating a single‑photon source, waveguide circuit and detectors on a chip, Rotonium builds on recent advances in silicon‑photonic qubits and could accelerate the path toward portable or data‑center quantum accelerators. The prototype’s four effective qubits are modest, so scaling fidelity and error correction remain open challenges, but the work signals that practical, scalable hardware may soon move beyond ultra‑cold labs.

Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — Rotonium has unveiled a quantum computer prototype that operates at room temperature, with no cryogenic cooling anywhere in the quantum chain: from the single-photon source to the processor and the detectors that read the results. item.title: Aalborg University Buys Quantum Computer to Train Engineers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it marks one of the first instances where a university is acquiring its own quantum processor primarily as an educational platform rather than a research workhorse, signaling a shift toward building a dedicated quantum‑engineer workforce. By giving students hands‑on experience with real hardware—rather than just cloud simulators—Aalborg University can accelerate curriculum development and align graduate skills with the growing industry demand seen in initiatives like IBM’s Q Network and Microsoft’s Azure Quantum. The impact will be felt most after the system arrives in 2027, but early exposure may give its graduates a competitive edge as quantum technologies move from prototype to commercial deployment.

Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — Aalborg University (AAU) is purchasing a quantum computer, which will be delivered and installed during 2027. item.title: Sorbonne Université and Qubit Pharmaceuticals Introduce VULCAN Hybrid Framework for Scalable Quantum Chemistry
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is noteworthy because VULCAN demonstrates that a carefully engineered hybrid workflow can slash the qubit‑count and measurement overhead traditionally required for chemically accurate simulations, moving quantum chemistry closer to near‑term hardware limits. By replacing the static operator pools of ADAPT‑VQE with a dynamic Lie‑algebraic generation scheme and compressing state overlaps on the fly, the framework leverages recent advances in adaptive ansätze while sidestepping their scaling bottlenecks. The reported benchmarks on larger molecular systems suggest that practical drug‑discovery calculations could become feasible on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices sooner than previously thought, though full validation on actual hardware and error mitigation strategies will still be needed.

Sorbonne Université and Qubit Pharmaceuticals developed VULCAN, a hybrid quantum-classical framework for quantum chemistry that overcomes limitations of ADAPT-VQE. VULCAN achieves chemical accuracy with significantly fewer quantum resources by employing techniques like dynamic Lie-algebraic operator pool generation, state-overlap circuit compression, and adaptive-subspace projection. Benchmarks show VULCAN outperforms batched ADAPT-VQE in terms of measurement cost and ability to reach chemical accuracy on complex molecules. item.title: Qubit Pharmaceuticals and Sorbonne Université Develop Polynomial-Time Lie Algebra Generator Pool Construction for Quantum Chemistry
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows a polynomial‑time method for constructing Minimal Complete Pools of Lie‑algebra generators, directly tackling the scaling bottleneck that has limited variational quantum eigensolvers in chemistry applications. By leveraging GPU acceleration on the Jean Zay supercomputer and releasing C++/CUDA verification tools, the work builds on recent adaptive‑ansatz research and gives practitioners a practical way to generate compact, expressive operator sets for near‑term hardware. The open‑source code lowers the barrier for other groups to test these pools, potentially speeding up molecular‑energy calculations that underpin drug‑discovery pipelines. Nonetheless, actual speedups on noisy quantum processors will still depend on qubit fidelity and effective error mitigation strategies.

Researchers from Qubit Pharmaceuticals and Sorbonne Université have developed a new method for quantum chemistry, introducing a polynomial-scaling algebraic framework to construct and verify Minimal Complete Pools (MCPs) for variational quantum eigensolvers (VQE). This approach significantly reduces computational overhead, as demonstrated by GPU-accelerated benchmarks on the Jean Zay supercomputer. The team has open-sourced their C++ and CUDA routines for MCP verification on GitHub. item.title: Qubit Pharmaceuticals, Sorbonne Université, and Q-CTRL Demonstrate 3D Protein Hydration-Site Prediction on IBM Heron Processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a near‑term quantum processor can tackle a concrete drug‑discovery subproblem—predicting where water molecules bind in a protein’s active site—by leveraging up to 123 qubits on IBM’s Heron chip and, in benchmark cases, finding lower‑energy configurations than classical heuristics. The result builds on the recent wave of quantum chemistry demonstrations (e.g., VQE studies of small molecules) by moving from isolated electronic structure calculations toward a biologically relevant, three‑dimensional optimization problem. While the authors estimate that around 900 qubits would be needed for routine pharmaceutical use, the work provides an early proof‑of‑concept that quantum hardware can already contribute to computer‑aided drug design and motivates continued scaling of error‑corrected processors.

Researchers from Qubit Pharmaceuticals, Sorbonne Université, and Q-CTRL successfully demonstrated 3D protein hydration-site prediction on IBM Heron quantum processors, utilizing up to 123 qubits to identify optimal water placements in drug-target proteins. Their quantum approach outperformed classical methods in certain scenarios, finding lower-energy solutions and achieving higher optimal sampling probabilities. This research paves the way for practical computer-aided drug discovery, with projections indicating utility with approximately 900 qubits. item.title: QuEra, Harvard, and UMD Researchers Develop Polynomial-Time Classical Benchmarking for Non-Clifford Fault-Tolerant Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first scalable classical tool for rigorously benchmarking the non‑Clifford components that make fault‑tolerant quantum computers universal, a task that has long been limited to small, brute‑force simulations. By turning arbitrary Pauli faults into Clifford operations and using Monte Carlo sampling, the method can evaluate logical fidelity on circuits with hundreds of physical qubits—far beyond prior capabilities—and it already highlights design choices such as shared ancilla blocks that boost magic‑state factory efficiency. In the broader landscape, the technique gives hardware teams at QuEra, IBM, Google and others a practical way to predict real‑world performance before costly experimental runs, accelerating the path toward usable error‑corrected processors. The results are still limited to circuits where the fault model fits the backpropagation scheme, so further extensions will be needed for more exotic noise sources.

Researchers developed a polynomial-time Monte Carlo method for benchmarking fault-tolerant non-Clifford quantum circuits, which are essential for universal quantum computation. This method efficiently simulates complex circuits and evaluates logical fidelity by backpropagating Pauli faults and reducing errors to Clifford operators. They demonstrated its effectiveness on circuits up to 256 physical qubits and various magic-state factory designs, finding that a shared ancilla block significantly improves efficiency. item.title: University of Innsbruck, ParityQC, and QuEra Turn Rydberg Array Embeddings into Intrinsic Error-Correcting Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the extra “auxiliary” atoms already present in neutral‑atom Rydberg processors can double as a built‑in classical error‑correcting code, turning what was previously overhead into a resource for more reliable optimization runs. By pairing this intrinsic code with a new Cluster decoder, the team demonstrated error‑correction thresholds above 23 % and rescued exact solutions on QuEra’s Aquila hardware that standard post‑processing missed—a milestone that narrows the gap between noisy analog devices and fault‑tolerant quantum advantage. The result dovetails with recent efforts to embed error mitigation directly into hardware architectures, suggesting a practical pathway for scaling neutral‑atom platforms without waiting for full quantum error correction. Readers should note, however, that the approach currently applies to combinatorial optimization embeddings rather than universal gate operations, so broader applicability will depend on future extensions of the technique.

Researchers from the University of Innsbruck, ParityQC, and QuEra have discovered that auxiliary qubits used in neutral-atom processors for combinatorial optimization problems inherently form a classical error-correcting code. They developed a Cluster decoder to work with this code, achieving error-correction thresholds of over 23% across various graph types. This method, validated on QuEra's Aquila processor, significantly improved the success rate of finding optimal solutions, even recovering exact solutions where raw hardware and other post-processing methods failed. item.title: University of California, QuEra, and Collaborators Introduce Multi-Agent LLM Compiler Qubrio for Neutral-Atom Processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases Qubrio, the first multi‑agent large‑language‑model compiler that can automatically place, route and schedule gates on neutral‑atom devices, a platform that has recently begun scaling to hundreds of qubits. By delivering noticeably lower circuit depth and higher fidelity than existing toolchains—and even inventing novel shuttling strategies—the work bridges the gap between hardware advances at QuEra and practical algorithm deployment, echoing similar AI‑driven compiler breakthroughs seen for superconducting chips. The result could accelerate experimental demonstrations of error‑corrected subroutines on neutral‑atom processors, though real‑world gains will still depend on how well the model adapts to evolving trap geometries and noise characteristics.

Researchers have introduced Qubrio, a multi-agent LLM compiler for neutral-atom quantum circuits, which automates qubit placement, routing, and schedule optimization. Qubrio significantly outperforms existing compilers, demonstrating faster execution, higher fidelity, and adaptability to various hardware configurations. The system also autonomously discovered efficient qubit shuttling techniques. item.title: QuEra Computing and Lawrence Berkeley National Lab Observe Prethermal Dynamical Phase Transitions on 180 Qubits in Nature Study
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a neutral‑atom processor can reliably explore non‑equilibrium many‑body physics on a scale (180 qubits) previously only accessible to classical supercomputers, confirming that prethermal dynamical phase transitions are not just theoretical curiosities but experimentally observable phenomena. By combining the Aquila hardware with state‑of‑the‑art simulations, the collaboration bridges the gap between quantum simulation and traditional computational methods, echoing recent advances from trapped‑ion and superconducting platforms in probing Floquet dynamics. The result underscores how near‑term quantum devices are becoming practical testbeds for complex condensed‑matter problems, although scaling to larger system sizes will still require improvements in coherence and error mitigation.

Researchers observed prethermal dynamical phase transitions on up to 180 qubits using QuEra's Aquila quantum processor. The study, published in Nature, details three phenomena: Floquet-like prethermal steady states, resonant melting, and a first-order dynamical phase transition in 2D. This work, a collaboration between QuEra, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, Harvard, and Boston University, utilized both quantum hardware and classical supercomputer simulations. item.title: Complex chaotic Boltzmann machines as deterministic representations of quantum states
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine can encode any pure quantum state as a deterministic trajectory in a high‑dimensional hypercube, extending the neural‑network wavefunction paradigm to a fully dynamical representation that captures both Born probabilities and relative phases. By turning the variational parameters of a network into the geometry of regular curves, islands and unstable regions, it offers a fresh way to visualise and explore phase information that is usually hidden in standard neural‑quantum‑state approaches—a capability that could sharpen variational algorithms and state‑tomography techniques. The work builds on recent successes of neural quantum states and tensor networks, but its reliance on low‑dimensional examples means further scaling studies will be needed before it can impact large‑scale quantum simulations.

Neural networks and tensor networks have opened new ways to explore quantum systems by parameterizing families of wave functions through the structure and parameters of a network. Here we extend this perspective to a dynamical representation: we introduce a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine that assigns a deterministic system to a pure quantum state. We extend Suzuki's construction to incorporate both Born probabilities and relative phases. The probabilities set the trajectory velocities in a hypercube, while the phases define a complex field that lifts its Poincare sections. The evolution is determined by the network parameters and initial conditions, without random choices during flights or configuration changes. Our analysis of two qubits and study of three-qubit families show how relations between probabilities organize regular curves, islands, and unstable regions, and how phases distinguish states that share the same Born dynamics. This architecture turns a wave-function parameterization into a geometry of trajectories, providing a tool to explore probabilities, phases, and symmetries together across families of states.

item.title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing obstacle for quantum annealers—efficiently handling linear constraints without inflating the problem into dense penalty graphs that quickly outstrip the sparse connectivity of current superconducting chips. By exploiting single‑shot spin‑fluctuation covariances to reconstruct dual curvature, the SelfCal‑QSQN scheme eliminates extra slack qubits and penalty couplers, enabling full‑chip feasibility on D‑Wave Advantage devices and delivering performance that rivals time‑matched mixed‑integer solvers at the 256‑spin scale. The result opens a realistic pathway for applying quantum annealing to real‑world constrained optimization in finance, power grids and logistics, though further work will be needed to confirm scalability beyond today’s few‑hundred‑qubit problems.

Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Detection of genuine multipartite entanglement by means of entanglement monotones
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a systematic way to construct genuine multipartite‑entanglement monotones that can certify “irreducible” D‑partite entanglement—states that cannot be broken down into lower‑order pieces—a capability that has been missing from most existing measures. By showing that no entropy‑based witness can satisfy both LOCC‑monotonicity and subadditivity, the authors motivate a relaxed LO‑monotone approach that nonetheless succeeds in detecting any form of genuine tripartite entanglement in three‑qubit systems, offering a powerful new benchmark for emerging quantum processors. The result dovetails with recent efforts to develop hardware‑friendly entanglement diagnostics and could help validate multi‑qubit gates and error‑correction codes once experimental protocols are built around these monotones.

We look for pure state entanglement monotones that may serve as certificates of a strong form of genuine multipartite entanglement, that we refer to as irreducible entanglement: a $D$-partite state (with $D\geq 3$) is irreducibly $D$-partite entangled if it cannot be decomposed as a product of states that are at most $(D-1)$-partite entangled. We start by establishing a no-go result proving that no reasonable genuine multipartite entanglement entropy can simultaneously obey LOCC-monotonicity and subadditivity. After relaxing the first condition to LO-monotonicity, we provide a simple method generating genuine multipartite entanglement monotones with the desired properties. Focusing on a subfamily of these monotones, we show that they are able to detect any form of genuine tripartite entanglement in three-qubit systems.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first ancilla‑free construction of exact Dicke‑state circuits that reaches both optimal linear gate count and logarithmic depth for any Hamming weight, a milestone because Dicke states are key resources for quantum metrology, error‑correcting codes and variational algorithms. By disproving the previously conjectured Ω(k) depth bound for balanced Dicke states, it shows that large‑scale symmetric entanglement can be generated far more efficiently than thought, opening the door to near‑term hardware demonstrations on modest qubit arrays. The constant‑time amplitude‑amplification step also means the method scales cleanly without costly iterative subroutines, although practical performance will still depend on native two‑qubit gate fidelity and connectivity. Readers should watch how this technique is adopted in quantum sensing prototypes and as a building block for more complex state‑preparation pipelines.

We construct exact circuits for $n$-qubit Dicke states of any Hamming weight $k$ using $O(n)$ single-qubit gates and CNOTs in $O(\log n)$ depth without ancillary qubits. The gate count and depth are asymptotically optimal for every $0<k<n$. We compress symmetric blocks to free output qubits for weight-dependent phases. A sign correction followed by a collective rotation produces a state whose overlap with the target is at least a positive constant, so exact amplitude amplification takes $O(1)$ steps. For balanced Dicke states ($k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$), the logarithmic depth disproves the $Ω(k)$ depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang (2025).

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics

item.title: Quantum control of an electrically levitated nanoparticle with a trapped ion
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single laser‑cooled ion can act as a quantum “refrigerator” and control hub for an electrically levitated nanoparticle, opening a realistic path to ground‑state cooling and non‑Gaussian state engineering of macroscopic objects. By exploiting parametric modulation of the Paul‑trap potential to resonantly enhance Coulomb coupling, the scheme builds on recent hybrid ion–nanoparticle experiments and complements optomechanical approaches that rely on optical tweezers, offering a fully electrical route with potentially lower photon‑scattering heating. If experimentally realized, such ion‑nanoparticle hybrids could become versatile testbeds for macroscopic quantum physics, precision sensing, and even modular quantum networking, although achieving the required trap stability and mitigating charge noise will be critical challenges.

Quantum control of levitated nanoparticles offers a route towards macroscopic quantum states. Here we propose a novel way to achieve it for a nanoparticle levitated electrically in a linear Paul trap together with a single ion, a system recently realized experimentally. By suitably engineering the trap's AC potential, one can parametrically modulate the ion-nanoparticle distance and thus the Coulomb coupling to enable a resonant interaction. For realistic parameters, we calculate that this enables sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle to its motional ground state by a single, continuously laser-cooled ion. Additional AC drives enable the preparation of squeezed nanoparticle states and of ion-nanoparticle entanglement. Moreover, non-Gaussian states such as Fock and cat states, prepared in the ion with standard trapped-ion techniques, can be transferred to the nanoparticle with high fidelities. We provide complete protocols for each of these states, including all known decoherence sources. Our results establish electrically trapped ion-nanoparticle systems as a platform for quantum control of levitated matter.

item.title: Navigating Quantum Education at the University level: Pedagogical Pathways and a Roadmap for Textbook Selection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the first systematic, cross‑textbook map of how quantum mechanics is introduced and sequenced at the university level, revealing five distinct entry‑point archetypes—including the newly identified “qubit‑first” pathway that aligns directly with emerging quantum‑computing curricula. By showing how identical topics can play very different pedagogical roles depending on their contextual framing, the study offers educators concrete guidance for designing courses that bridge mathematical rigor, experimental intuition, and computational relevance—a need sharpened by the rapid expansion of quantum‑technology programs worldwide. The roadmap also gives institutions a practical tool for selecting or adapting textbooks to produce graduates who can more readily transition into research labs or industry teams building real quantum hardware.

Instruction in quantum mechanics (QM) is often categorized by its entry point as 'wave-first' or 'spin-first', yet these labels lack consistent definitions and overlook other established or emerging approaches. Moreover, while capturing broad differences in topic selection and sequencing, this binary framing obscures critical differences in contextualization--how three dimensions (mathematical tools, phenomena and experiments, and theoretical concepts) are framed and connected to support student sensemaking. Research also rarely examines how such pedagogical choices unfold across the undergraduate-to-graduate trajectory. Using textbooks as an analytical lens to map these choices and characterize overarching pathways, encompassing entry points and overall orientations, we comparatively analyze the selection, sequencing, and contextualization of core topics across these 3 dimensions, alongside prefaces and introductions, in 36 university QM textbooks spanning countries and eras. At the topic level, we show that identical topics occupy widely different curricular roles depending on their contextualization. Synthesizing these findings into pathways, we identify three additional entry-point archetypes (labeled path-, qubit-, and axiom-first) and characterize all 5 approaches, showing that most textbooks combine multiple archetypes in their opening chapters. Extending this synthesis beyond entry points, we map textbooks' overall orientations relative to mathematics, experiment and application, and theoretical physics. Interpreting these profiles alongside authors' rationales reveals how educators navigate competing trade-offs among mathematical accessibility, theoretical generality, physical motivation, and modern developments. This study provides a multidimensional framework, substantive examples, and a practical roadmap for textbook selection and curriculum design in QM education.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Classical simulability and hardware diagnostics for QAOA on geographic coverage benchmarks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a carefully crafted classical reference can expose hidden shortcomings in QAOA performance, revealing that the modest energy reductions observed on a 24‑qubit device are largely reproduced by an uncorrelated product distribution rather than genuine quantum correlations. By demonstrating that a larger, exactly simulable 51‑qubit encoding preserves the problem’s structure while remaining tractable blockwise, the work provides a practical diagnostic toolkit for distinguishing true algorithmic progress from artefacts of benchmark design. The approach builds on recent efforts to benchmark variational algorithms with realistic hardware constraints and offers a concrete method for researchers to validate whether observed improvements reflect quantum advantage or merely statistical noise. It cautions practitioners that without such diagnostics, optimistic claims about QAOA scalability could be misleading.

Quantum-optimization benchmarks can show reduced energy while concealing local loss of weighted covariance. We combine encoding checks with exact structural references to select informative circuit diagnostics for static geographic coverage instances. The executed 24-qubit surrogate has infeasible ground states, whereas a faithful 51-qubit slack encoding preserves its 13 support-graph components and remains exactly simulable blockwise. At the executed angles, the total ideal optimum probability is $5.47\times10^{-20}$, making optimum counts uninformative at the executed budget of $10^5$ shots. A product distribution with the measured bit marginals accounts for about $90\%$ of the observed energy reduction. In three fixed-circuit jobs, the global weighted-covariance ratio is approximately $0.50$, while a five-variable block has ratios between $0.12$ and $0.28$ and contributes only $3.7\%$ of the ideal global denominator. Simultaneous bands resolve its deficit relative to the global ratio under an exploratory conditional counting model. The exact block reference thus reveals a local discrepancy concealed by the aggregate, without identifying an error mechanism or establishing device stability. The procedure links benchmark structure to the resolution and limitations of its observables.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the “exponential concentration” bottleneck that has been limiting the scalability of quantum machine‑learning models, a problem closely related to the barren‑plateau phenomenon identified in recent variational‑circuit studies. By systematically comparing fidelity‑based kernels, projected kernels and quantum extreme learning across locality, entanglement and circuit depth, the authors show that bandwidth scaling can temper concentration in moderately expressive regimes, offering a practical knob for designers of near‑term QML algorithms. The work therefore provides concrete guidance on how to balance encoding expressivity against measurement sensitivity, an insight that will be valuable as researchers move from proof‑of‑concept kernels toward larger, hardware‑friendly quantum learning pipelines.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

item.title: Guest Post: When Will Quantum Computing Become Useful for Insurance?

item.title: Quantum-Chaos-Assisted Measure Synchronization in a Double-Well Ultracold Bose Gas
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that quantum chaotic dynamics can dramatically accelerate measure synchronization in a double‑well Bose‑Einstein condensate, revealing a direct link between chaos, rapid synchronization and high entanglement entropy. The finding suggests a new route for fast state preparation or stabilization in analog quantum simulators, complementing recent advances in Floquet engineering and dissipative control of many‑body systems. This paper investigates measure synchronization (MS) in a two-component ultracold atomic system confined in a double-well potential, which realizes a quantum many-body bosonic Josephson junction. Through spectral-statistics analysis, we identify the quantum chaotic parameter regime and confirm that the system achieves MS within this regime with weak dependence on the initial energy imbalance. We further show that chaotic dynamics not only significantly shortens the time scale for establishing synchronization but is also accompanied by entanglement entropy approaching the random-state prediction. These results reveal close connections among quantum chaos, MS, and quantum entanglement in conservative quantum many-body systems and may motivate further studies on the underlying mechanisms of chaos-assisted synchronization.

item.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward usable quantum differential‑equation solvers by delivering an end‑to‑end pipeline that starts from classical data and returns classical observables for the linearized Poisson‑Boltzmann equation, a workhorse in biomolecular modeling. By introducing a new grid representation for variable‑coefficient PDEs and leveraging wavelet preconditioning, the authors achieve polylogarithmic gate complexity in both problem size and target precision—eliminating the condition‑number bottleneck that has hampered earlier proposals. If fault‑tolerant hardware catches up, such an approach could give quantum computers a practical edge in high‑resolution electrostatic simulations for drug discovery and protein engineering.

Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

item.title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a party’s geographic position can serve as the authentication credential in BB84‑based quantum key distribution, dramatically cutting the overhead by interleaving lightweight quantum‑position‑verification rounds instead of running a full QPV protocol for every bit. By marrying QKD with location‑based security, it tackles one of the most practical hurdles—efficient, trustworthy authentication—and dovetails with recent pushes toward measurement‑device‑independent and satellite‑based QKD where spatial information is already a key resource. The authors’ initial security analysis covers only a restricted class of attacks, so broader composable proofs will be needed before deployment, but the approach points to a promising route for scaling authenticated quantum communications.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

item.title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that modest quantum error‑detecting codes—especially two‑qubit repetition or parity encodings—can already give a measurable boost to long‑distance, trust‑free QKD when deployed in sequential repeater chains, narrowing the gap between today’s noisy hardware and fully fault‑tolerant networks. By rigorously comparing entanglement‑generation architectures and quantifying how incremental improvements in memory lifetimes or photon‑collection efficiencies translate into higher secret‑key rates, the work connects directly to ongoing experimental efforts on fiber‑based repeaters and satellite links. The findings suggest that near‑term quantum‑communication deployments may not need heavyweight error correction, but rather a carefully chosen lightweight code plus targeted hardware upgrades, offering a realistic pathway toward scalable quantum networks.

Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

item.title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
item.description:
Curator's Take: This work overturns a long‑standing assumption that nuisance parameters must be locally suppressed in error‑corrected quantum sensors, showing instead that only Markovian noise needs active correction while coherent control can simply separate unwanted drifts from the signal over the full interrogation time. By proving a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg‑limited precision under realistic Hamiltonian dynamics, the authors expand the parameter regimes where quadratic scaling is achievable—an advance that could immediately inform the design of next‑generation atomic clocks, magnetometers, and distributed sensor networks. The result also clarifies why recent experiments using dynamical decoupling or tailored pulse sequences have succeeded despite residual systematic drifts, pointing to a broader, more flexible blueprint for robust quantum metrology.

Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

item.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the classical side of fault‑tolerant quantum computing can finally keep pace with today’s fast superconducting processors by delivering a decoder that is both sub‑microsecond and dramatically more accurate than existing real‑time solutions. By co‑designing a neural network to run on an FPGA in integer arithmetic, the Rapids decoder cuts logical error rates by two orders of magnitude while preserving the low latency required for surface‑code cycles, directly reducing the qubit overhead that has limited scalable experiments. The demonstrated scalability across multiple FPGAs and the path toward ASIC implementation signal that classical hardware will become a first‑class resource in future quantum architectures, easing one of the biggest bottlenecks on the road to practical error correction.

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a subtle but critical security gap in entanglement‑swapping repeaters by showing that dishonest nodes can hide misreported measurement outcomes behind ordinary readout noise, making standard verification ineffective. By introducing a cut‑and‑choose certification scheme that tests only a random subset while preserving the remaining pairs for use, it offers a realistic quality‑of‑service guarantee compatible with emerging quantum‑network protocols. The analysis also highlights today’s memory bottleneck—certifying even a modest 1 % misreport rate on a million links would require storing up to a million entangled pairs—underscoring the need for scalable quantum memories before such safeguards can be deployed at scale.

Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

item.title: Tunable Ground-State Entanglement in Fully Connected Quantum Systems: From Logarithmic to Volume-Law Scaling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by simply tweaking the strength‑scaling exponent of all‑to‑all couplings, one can continuously dial a system’s ground‑state entanglement from the familiar logarithmic bound up to a full volume law, something previously thought impossible for gapped, nondegenerate states. The result bridges theoretical work on Kac‑normalized models with the practical reality of hardware platforms such as trapped‑ion and superconducting arrays that naturally exhibit long‑range interactions, offering a new knob to engineer entanglement complexity without changing the underlying connectivity. It also warns that even modest departures from the canonical normalization can erase universal entanglement limits, a consideration that will matter for designing scalable quantum simulators and error‑corrected architectures.

Entanglement scaling is a central probe of the complexity of quantum many-body ground states, yet once geometric locality is absent, it can depend sensitively on the structure and normalization of interactions. For fully connected Hamiltonians with the natural Kac normalization, nondegenerate gapped ground states are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound. Here we ask how the ground-state entanglement changes when this interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale. We answer this question by constructing an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-κ}$. For sufficiently small fixed coupling, we prove that every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $Θ(n^{2-2κ} \log n)$ for $1/2<κ\leq1$ and $Θ(n)$ at $κ=1/2$. We further show that the ground state is unique and separated from the rest of the spectrum by a system-size-independent gap for $3/4 \leq κ\leq 1$, while weak-coupling analysis and numerical calculations suggest that the gap remains open also for $1/2 \leq κ< 3/4$. Thus, varying only the interaction normalization yields a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization $κ=1$ to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law, showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of this normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

item.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the long‑standing simplification of circuit‑level noise into binary detector error models can be lifted without sacrificing decoding simplicity, by representing each fault location with a single non‑binary random variable that captures the full Pauli alphabet. The resulting non‑binary DEMs exactly describe any Clifford‑based syndrome extraction circuit, produce Tanner graphs with dramatically fewer edges and improve decoder performance on surface, color and bicycle codes—an advance that directly addresses the scalability bottlenecks highlighted in recent Stim and fault‑tolerant QEC studies. By keeping belief‑propagation messages scalar, the approach promises more hardware‑friendly decoders while preserving—or even enhancing—the error‑suppression needed for practical quantum computers.

A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

item.title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a concrete way to put the timing of measurements themselves into a quantum superposition, turning the classic Quantum Zeno effect into a probe of relational time that can be realized on today’s superconducting‑qubit platforms. By showing that interference between two distinct measurement schedules depends only on their relative offset—and that a single schedule can even reverse the usual Zeno freezing— the work opens a new experimental handle for testing foundational ideas while also suggesting novel sensing schemes where timing coherence boosts resolution. The authors back up the proposal with realistic gate counts and error budgets, making it a timely bridge between abstract Page‑Wootters concepts and near‑term hardware demonstrations.

Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

item.title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates for the first time how a simple, exactly solvable qubit chain can separate the spread of entanglement from the emergence of locally readable information, revealing that weak interactions let quantum correlations outrun any measurable record on a neighboring site. By showing that off‑diagonal elements of a reduced density matrix serve as the leading “record” detectable with a single Pauli measurement—and by quantifying optimal recovery fidelities when only a fragment of the environment is accessible—the work bridges fundamental studies of decoherence with practical concerns in quantum error correction and sensor design. The finding that intra‑environment interactions can reshuffle readable records without altering the system’s reduced state suggests new strategies for engineering protective environments that preserve recoverable information while minimizing disturbance to the processor itself.

We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

item.title: Quantum Autoencoder on Real Hardware for New Physics Searches at Muon Colliders
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first demonstrations that a quantum autoencoder can be run on real‑world hardware to tackle a high‑energy physics problem, showing that a six‑qubit circuit on the Tianyan176 processor already distinguishes Standard Model tri‑photon events from anomalous quartic gauge‑coupling signatures. By delivering reconstruction‑loss based discrimination comparable to classical analyses, it highlights how near‑term quantum machine‑learning tools could become part of the data‑analysis pipeline for future muon colliders, where massive event rates will demand ultra‑efficient pattern recognition. The work also underscores current limitations—noise and qubit count still constrain scalability—but sets a clear benchmark for how quantum‑enhanced searches for new physics might evolve as hardware improves.

We apply a quantum autoencoder to search for new physics (NP) in the tri-photon process $μ^+μ^-\toγγγ$ at muon colliders. Using a six-qubit circuit on the Tianyan176 quantum computer, we measure the reconstruction losses for Standard Model (SM) events and anomalous quartic gauge couplings (aQGCs) events. The results demonstrate that the hardware-implemented quantum autoencoder effectively discriminates NP signals from the SM background. Concurrently, we derive the expected constraints on the aQGCs coefficients and compare them with those obtained from conventional methods.

item.title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first quantitative link between a fundamental notion of “irrealism” – how far measurement outcomes deviate from having pre‑existing values – and the performance of quantum random access codes, a benchmark task for communication‑limited quantum processors. By mapping out exact irrealism frontiers for both prepare‑and‑measure and entanglement‑assisted schemes, it shows that modest amounts of nonclassical disturbance are sufficient to surpass classical success rates, while higher advantages demand genuine realism‑based nonlocality in the shared resource. The results give experimentalists a concrete metric for assessing how much coherence or entanglement their hardware must retain to achieve a target QRAC advantage, and they clarify why simply using mutually unbiased bases is not always the most resource‑efficient strategy.

How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

item.title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how logical Pauli‑product measurements can be carried out across multiple code blocks without adding any extra data qubits, a step that could dramatically cut the overhead of fault‑tolerant architectures beyond the surface code. By framing the measurement as a “code quilt” built from subsystem‑code gauge generators, the authors demonstrate concrete circuits that keep physical qubit degree low and preserve code‑capacity distance in extensive simulations on bicycle and surface codes. While the first variant is not provably fault tolerant at asymptotic distances and the second lacks a general proof, the empirical results suggest a practical pathway toward more resource‑efficient error correction and multi‑code logical operations.

Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

item.title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article proves that any non‑contextual Pauli Hamiltonian is secretly a free‑fermion model, establishing a concrete bridge between contextual subspace decompositions and the well‑understood physics of free fermions. By formalising the proof in Lean and delivering a heuristic line‑graph algorithm to pull out free‑fermion fragments from molecular Hamiltonians, it gives practitioners a new, classically tractable way to carve up problems before handing them to a quantum processor. The result could shrink the quantum workload for chemistry simulations by allowing larger portions of the Hamiltonian to be solved exactly on classical hardware, although its effectiveness will depend on how often realistic molecules admit the required graph structure.

Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.
